question: Do the euro-coin data give evidence that the coin is biased rather than fair, and how do we compute that with Bayes factors?
contributions: Bayes factor as likelihood ratio p(D|B)/p(D|F)
Shows B must be defined without looking at the data, as a suite of sub-hypotheses whose likelihood is the prior-weighted average
Jeffreys scale and an odds reading of Bayes factors

results.claim: Bayes factor for B_uniform (uniform prior over x, 50 removed) against F is below 1, so the data weakly favour the fair coin.
results.setup: Euro problem (MacKay): Belgian one-euro coin spun on edge 250 times, 140 heads, 110 tails; F = fair (x=50%), B = biased; Bayes factor = p(D|B)/p(D|F)
results.quote: The likelihood ratio for b_uniform is 0.47

results.claim: The B_cheat hypothesis (x set to the observed 140/250) gives Bayes factor 6.1, but is bogus because the hypothesis uses the data.
results.setup: Euro problem (MacKay): Belgian one-euro coin spun on edge 250 times, 140 heads, 110 tails; F = fair (x=50%), B = biased; Bayes factor = p(D|B)/p(D|F)

results.claim: B_two (x is 0.4 or 0.6, equal weight) gives weak evidence for biased.
results.setup: Euro problem (MacKay): Belgian one-euro coin spun on edge 250 times, 140 heads, 110 tails; F = fair (x=50%), B = biased; Bayes factor = p(D|B)/p(D|F)
results.quote: The likelihood ratio (or Bayes factor) for b_two is 1.3

results.claim: B_triangle (triangle prior peaking at 50%) gives weak evidence against biased.

results.claim: Likelihood of the data under the fair coin is tiny, so only the ratio is informative.

Bayes factor 100 from 1:1 prior odds gives posterior odds 100:1, over 99%.

results.claim: The newspaper quoted a frequentist statement that an unbiased coin would give a result this extreme with chance under 7%.

results.claim: The verdict depends on how B is specified; with different definitions the evidence is for or against, but always weak, other than the cheating definition.

limits: The chapter says the specification of B depends on background information, so people could reasonably disagree about the right definition.
Evidence in every non-cheating version is weak; Jeffreys' adjectives are historical and the chapter prefers thinking in odds.
Code is Python 2 era (xrange, thinkbayes Suite classes); the Likelihood snippet has a heads/head typo as printed.
Exercises 11.1-11.2 raise but do not answer whether a Bayes factor of 1000 should overcome a very low prior for ESP.
practices: Define the alternative hypothesis B before looking at the data; a hypothesis built from the data (B_cheat) makes any dataset favour B (11.1).
Treat a composite hypothesis as a suite of sub-hypotheses and compute its likelihood as the prior-weighted average of sub-likelihoods (11.2).
The return value of Suite.Update/Normalize is that average likelihood, so it can replace a separate SuiteLikelihood function (11.2).
Interpret Bayes factors as odds multipliers on prior odds rather than arguing about adjectives (11.4).
Compare the Bayes factor against modelling error: a factor of 2 moves 50% to 66% and is small for most real problems (11.4).

terms.definition: likelihood ratio of the data under a hypothesis versus the alternative; greater than 1 means data favour the hypothesis
biased hypothesis with x set to the observed 140/250; bogus because it uses the data
1-3 barely worth mentioning; 3-10 substantial; 10-30 strong; 30-100 very strong; >100 decisive
